threads.thread_goal: Align on current workflows and main pain points across all service types.

messages.text: Kicking off Field Service Workflow Standardisation for Repair Operations. I have uploaded the first pass of Current Repair Workflow Maps under project_pack_ref: Field Service Workflow Standardisation for Repair Operations as A1, based on interviews and notes from the last two weeks. This should also close the mapping part of T1 at draft level.  Quick ask for everyone: 1) Scan your area in A1 and call out anything that looks off or missing. 2) List the top pain points you see today in your day-to-day work.  For now I have grouped flows into: in-home appliance repairs, workshop power tool repairs, telecom / consumer electronics visits, and heavy item moves to and from the workshop.  Once we agree on the main issues, we will lock the focus for the first SOP version and the pilot scope.  Please reply in this thread with your view by tomorrow so we can converge on the top three problems and confirm which service types go into the initial pilot.

Looked at the in-home appliance repair flow in A1. A couple of things from my side:  - Intake: we often get incomplete problem descriptions from customer service, so the first visit is sometimes just confirming the issue. That is not really shown in the map.  - Parts: the step where we check van stock vs ordering parts is there, but in practice we often drive back to the workshop because we do not have the right part. That adds a lot of extra time and second visits.  - Paper forms: the safety checks on the paper form are not always filled in because they are at the bottom and we are in a rush.  Pain points I see most: 1) Rework due to missing parts. 2) Time lost on the road between jobs. 3) Confusion on who calls the customer when we are delayed.  Let me know if you want me to add more detail to A1 for the appliance section.

I went through the workshop power tool repair flow in A1. The main steps look right, but a few gaps from what I see on the bench:  - Diagnostic is shown as a single box. In reality we do visual inspection, insulation and continuity checks, then functional tests under load. When we skip the structured order, we miss issues and tools come back.  - There is no explicit step for checking if the customer uses the tool in a way that causes repeat failures. We sometimes find misuse only after the second or third repair.  - The handover from movers to workshop is a bit simplified. Sometimes tools arrive without proper labels or fault description, which slows us down.  Top pain points for me: 1) Inconsistent diagnostics leading to rework. 2) Poor information on intake from the field or movers. 3) No clear rule on when to call the customer for approval if we find extra damage.  These are all things a standard checklist and SOP could help with.

I checked the power tool part of A1 as well. It mostly matches what I do, but I am not sure about the order of some steps. For example, the map shows functional test before opening the housing, but sometimes I open first if the tool looks damaged. Maybe we should clarify that.  Pain points I notice: - Sometimes I am not sure which electrical tests are mandatory vs optional. - The form for logging readings is not very clear, so I skip some fields. - When movers bring tools, I do not always know if they were dropped or mishandled during transport.  I can help update A1 if someone guides me on the right sequence we want to standardise.

On the telecom and consumer electronics side, A1 is close but a bit too generic. A few specifics:  - Pre-visit checks: we always run a line test or signal check from the office before going out, and that is missing. It helps avoid unnecessary visits.  - On-site, we have a standard order: visual inspection, wiring check, signal measurement with the meter, then configuration of the device. The map mixes configuration and measurement.  - There is no explicit step for logging readings and configuration changes. Right now, people do it differently, and we lose data for troubleshooting.  My top pain points: 1) Lack of consistent logging of readings and configs. 2) Last-minute schedule changes that cause rushed visits and shortcuts. 3) No clear rule on when to escalate complex cases vs trying to fix everything on-site.  These will be important when we define T4 and later A4.

From the moving side, the flow in A1 shows pick up, transport, and drop off, but it misses some details that cause trouble:  - Sometimes we get heavy or fragile items without clear instructions on how they should be packed or lifted. That leads to delays while we figure it out, or risk of damage.  - The handover with technicians is not always at the same point. Sometimes we wait on-site for them, sometimes we just leave items in the workshop. That affects our route planning.  - There is no standard way to record if something was already damaged before we touch it. That can create disputes later.  Pain points I see: 1) Lack of clear handling instructions for heavy or fragile equipment. 2) Unpredictable timing for handovers with technicians. 3) Limited coordination between our route plan and the technicians schedule.  These link directly to T6 and later A6, and also to T5 for scheduling rules.

Thanks for the detailed notes on the appliance flow. I will update A1 to reflect:  - An explicit step for clarifying the problem on-site when the intake is incomplete.  - A decision point on parts: check van stock vs order vs return to workshop, with a flag for potential second visit.  - A clearer safety check step earlier in the visit so it is not buried at the bottom of the paper form.  On pain points, I am hearing: missing parts, travel time, and unclear ownership of customer updates. These are strong candidates for our top three. I will wait for others to weigh in before we lock them for D1.

Good catch on the diagnostic detail. For the next revision of A1, I will break out the power tool diagnostic into visual, electrical, and functional steps, which will also feed directly into T3 and later A3.  On your pain points: inconsistent diagnostics, poor intake info, and unclear customer approval rules are very aligned with what we want to fix. They also connect to T7 and A7 for communication.  I suggest we treat inconsistent diagnostics and poor intake information as part of the same broader problem: lack of standardised checklists and forms. That would be one of the three main issues we tackle first.

On the telecom and electronics flow, I will adjust A1 to add:  - A pre-visit remote test step.  - A clearer order of on-site checks: visual, wiring, measurement, then configuration.  - A dedicated logging step for readings and configuration changes, which will later map into T4 and A4.  Your pain points around logging, schedule changes, and escalation rules fit well with the themes we have: standardising diagnostic steps, scheduling and logistics, and exception handling.  I will propose a draft list of top pain points in a bit so we can confirm D1.

For the moving flow, I will extend A1 with:  - A step to check and record pre-existing damage before loading.  - A standard decision on whether movers wait for technicians or drop off at the workshop, which will later be governed by T5 and A5.  - A placeholder for handling instructions that will be detailed in T6 and A6.  Your pain points around handling instructions, handover timing, and coordination with technician schedules are strong inputs for both the scheduling rules and the handling checklist.

On the top issues, from the appliance side I agree that missing parts and unclear customer updates are big ones. Travel time is also painful, but sometimes it is just traffic. Maybe the bigger thing we can control is how we plan routes and time slots.  For the pilot, I think in-home appliance repairs should definitely be in scope, since we touch most of the pain points there: diagnostics, scheduling, and communication. I am fine if we start with a subset of appliance jobs, like standard washing machines and fridges, to keep it manageable.

Grouping inconsistent diagnostics and poor intake info under one broader problem makes sense to me. From the bench, it feels like the same root cause: no standard way to capture and use information from the first contact through to the repair.  On the pilot scope, I would like workshop power tool repairs included, at least for the most common tools like drills and grinders. That is where a structured checklist will show quick impact on rework. We can keep more complex tools out of the first round if needed.

I support including telecom and consumer electronics visits in the initial pilot, but maybe limited to standard installs and basic fault calls. Complex network issues could stay out until we have proven the basics.  On the top issues, I would phrase them as: 1) Lack of standard diagnostic and logging steps across all service types. 2) Weak scheduling and coordination between technicians and movers. 3) Inconsistent customer communication around delays, approvals, and follow-ups.  That seems to cover what everyone has raised so far.

I agree with that list of main problems. From the moving side, the second one about scheduling and coordination is the biggest. If we fix that, a lot of the waiting time and rushed jobs will improve.  For the pilot scope, I suggest we include moves related to the same appliance and power tool jobs that are in scope, plus standard workshop transfers. That way we can test T5 and later A5 properly without touching every single route we run.

On the pilot, I am ok if we start with the common power tools like drills and grinders, as mentioned. It will also make it easier for me to follow a clear sequence once T3 and A3 are defined.  For the top issues, I do feel the lack of clear steps and forms every day, so I support the three main problems that were summarised. I do not have anything to add beyond what has been said.

Let me summarise what I am hearing so we can close D1 and D2.  Proposed top three problems for the first SOP version: 1) No standard diagnostic and logging steps across service types, leading to rework and poor data. 2) Weak scheduling and coordination between technicians and movers, causing travel waste and waiting time. 3) Inconsistent customer communication on delays, approvals, and follow-ups.  Proposed initial pilot scope: - In-home appliance repairs for standard washing machines and fridges. - Workshop power tool repairs for common tools like drills and grinders. - Telecom and consumer electronics visits limited to standard installs and basic faults. - Moves directly linked to those jobs plus standard workshop transfers.  Unless there are strong objections, I will record these as our agreed focus and pilot scope for D1 and D2 and update A1 and T1 accordingly.
The summary and pilot scope work for me. The three main problems match what I see in the workshop, and the pilot coverage for power tools is realistic. Happy to proceed on that basis.
No objections from my side. The three focus areas are clear, and the telecom and electronics pilot scope is manageable. Please go ahead and update A1 and T1 with these decisions.

threads.thread_goal: Define and iterate on diagnostic checklists for appliances and power tools.

messages.text: Following the alignment on main problems and pilot scope, I have drafted first versions of the Standard Appliance Diagnostic Checklist and the Power Tool Repair Checklist, stored as A2 and A3 under project_pack_ref: Field Service Workflow Standardisation for Repair Operations. These drafts are based on A1 and the inputs you shared, and they map to T2 and T3.  Structure: - A2: intake, safety, diagnostic, repair, testing, and parts/time fields for in-home appliance jobs. - A3: visual inspection, electrical tests, functional tests, and notes for both corded and battery tools.  I need your feedback on two things: 1) Are the steps complete enough for day-to-day work? 2) What is the minimum set of steps we must always follow, even on a busy day?  Once we agree on the minimum required steps, we will record D3 and D4 and move to pilot-ready versions. Please comment with concrete changes or concerns.

I reviewed A2. Overall it looks usable, but I have a few comments:  - Intake: could we add a simple field to note if the customer description was clear or not? That helps explain longer visits.  - Safety: the checklist has several safety checks, but on a busy day it is hard to remember all. Maybe we can highlight the absolute must-do items, like power isolation and leak checks.  - Diagnostic: there are many possible tests. For common issues like no power or not draining, could we group the basic checks together so we do not miss them?  For minimum steps, I would say: confirm model and serial, run the key safety checks, perform at least the basic diagnostic steps for the reported symptom, and do a final functional test. If we try to make everything mandatory, people might skip the form.

On A3, I like that it separates visual, electrical, and functional checks. A few detailed suggestions:  - Visual inspection: add explicit checks for cord damage, housing cracks, and signs of overheating around vents. These are quick but catch a lot of issues.  - Electrical tests: for corded tools, I would make insulation resistance and continuity mandatory. For battery tools, we should add a simple battery voltage and internal resistance check.  - Functional tests: we should always test under load where safe, not just free running. Maybe add a field to note the type of load used.  For minimum steps, I would define: visual inspection items, core electrical tests (adapted for corded vs battery), and at least one functional test under load. Optional steps can cover deeper diagnostics for complex faults. That should be enough to reduce rework without slowing us down too much.

I went through A3 as well. Some of the test names are a bit technical for me. For example, I am not always sure when to use each electrical test or what values are acceptable.  Could we add a short hint next to each mandatory test, like what tool to use and what a normal reading looks like? That would help me follow the checklist correctly.  For minimum steps, I agree with the idea of always doing visual, basic electrical, and a functional test. I just need clearer guidance so I do not skip or misinterpret anything.

Good points on A2. I will adjust the draft as follows:  - Add a field in the intake section to flag if the customer description is clear or unclear.  - Mark a small subset of safety checks as must-do for every job, visually separated from the nice-to-have items.  - Group basic diagnostic steps by common symptom, starting with no power and not draining, so the flow is easier to follow.  For the minimum required steps for D3, I propose: 1) Confirm appliance identification (model and serial). 2) Complete all must-do safety checks. 3) Perform the basic diagnostic steps for the reported symptom. 4) Record parts used and estimated vs actual time. 5) Run and record a final functional test.  Let me know if this set feels realistic for daily use before we lock it in.

On A3, I will incorporate your suggestions:  - Add explicit visual checks for cord, housing, and overheating marks.  - For corded tools, make insulation resistance and continuity mandatory.  - For battery tools, add mandatory battery voltage and internal resistance checks.  - Require at least one functional test under load where safe, with a field to describe the load.  For D4, I suggest we define the minimum required steps as: 1) Complete all visual inspection items. 2) Perform the mandatory electrical tests for the tool type (corded or battery). 3) Run at least one functional test under load and record the result.  Optional steps can cover deeper diagnostics.  Please confirm if this matches what you had in mind.

Yes, that matches my intent. The three groups you listed for D4 cover the essentials. As long as the checklist clearly separates mandatory from optional steps, it should work well in the workshop.  One more detail: for tools that cannot be safely tested under load, we should allow a note explaining why the load test was skipped, so it does not look like a mistake.

The minimum set you proposed for A2 sounds workable. Highlighting the must-do safety checks will help a lot. I also like the idea of grouping diagnostics by symptom.  I agree that confirming model and serial, doing the must-do safety checks, running the basic diagnostic steps for the symptom, recording parts and time, and doing a final test should be mandatory. I am ok with you recording that as the minimum for D3.

If we add short hints next to each mandatory electrical test in A3, I am comfortable with the minimum steps you described. The three groups are clear enough for me to follow.  I also support adding a note field when a load test cannot be done safely, as mentioned. That will avoid confusion later when someone reviews the checklist.

Understood. I will add a mandatory note field in A3 when a load test is skipped, so it is clear that it was a conscious decision.  Given the feedback from both of you, I will update T3 and A3 to reflect:  - Mandatory visual checks.  - Mandatory electrical tests per tool type.  - Functional test under load or documented reason if not possible.  I will treat this as the agreed minimum for D4 unless someone raises a concern today.

Great, thanks for confirming. I will now:  - Update A2 to highlight must-do safety checks and group diagnostics by symptom.  - Mark the following as the minimum required steps for D3 in T2: confirm model and serial, complete must-do safety checks, run basic diagnostic steps for the reported symptom, record parts and estimated vs actual time, and perform a final functional test.  This will give us a clear baseline for the appliance part of the pilot.

No further concerns from me. Once you push the updated A3, I will start using it on a few jobs informally before the official pilot, so we can spot any obvious gaps early. I will note any issues for T11 later.

threads.thread_goal: Agree on telecom/electronics visit SOP and safety/handling procedures.

messages.text: I have drafted the telecom and consumer electronics service visit procedure as A4, based on A1 and the earlier discussion. It covers pre-visit checks, on-site installation and repair, and signal testing, and it aligns with T4.  Key sections in A4:  - Pre-visit: remote line or signal test, check of customer history, and confirmation of required equipment.  - On-site: visual inspection, wiring check, signal measurement with the meter, configuration of devices, and customer handover.  - Logging: mandatory recording of readings and configuration changes, plus notes on any escalations.  In parallel, we need to align with the handling and transport safety checklist A6 that 319539 is shaping under T6, so that telecom and electronics equipment is moved safely.  Please review A4 and A6 and comment on any missing steps or safety concerns before we sign off for pilot use.

On A6, I have put together a draft checklist for handling and transport of heavy or fragile equipment, linked to T6. It includes:  - Packing: choosing the right packaging, padding, and securing small parts.  - Lifting: checking weight, using proper lifting techniques, and using equipment like dollies or cranes when needed.  - Securing: how to stack and secure items in the vehicle to avoid movement.  - Handover: steps to record pre-existing damage and confirm condition with technicians at pickup and drop-off.  I tried to keep it practical so it fits into our current paper forms. Please let me know if there are telecom-specific items we should add, like extra protection for signal equipment or cables.

Thanks for pulling A4 and A6 together. From a project view, we need to make sure:  - A4 clearly states which readings must always be logged for the pilot, so we can feed T9 and T10 later.  - A6 is aligned with our safety constraints, especially for lifting and electrical equipment.  I will review both against the project constraints and safety notes, but I would like to hear from you on any edge cases that might not fit the standard flow, so we can add an exception handling section before we sign off D5 and D6.

On A4, the main edge cases I see are:  - Complex interference issues where we need specialised tools or a second visit. For those, we should have a clear rule to stop after basic checks and log an escalation.  - Unsafe environments on-site, like exposed wiring or unstable ladders. In those cases, the SOP should say we stop work, record the risk, and inform the customer and operations.  For mandatory readings, I suggest we always log: signal strength, signal-to-noise ratio where applicable, and any configuration changes made to modems, routers, or set-top boxes. That will give us enough data for T9 and T10 without overloading the form.  If we add these points, I am comfortable using A4 in the pilot.

For A6, a few edge cases:  - Very heavy racks or cabinets that exceed manual lifting limits. In those cases, the checklist should require mechanical aids or an extra person, and allow us to refuse the move if that is not possible.  - Fragile electronics with loose parts. We should have a step to ask technicians to secure internal components or remove modules before transport when needed.  - Moves in tight staircases or spaces. The checklist should remind us to assess the route and, if it is unsafe, to stop and call operations for a different plan.  If we include these, I think A6 will cover most of what we see in the field.

From a telecom perspective, A6 should also mention:  - Avoiding sharp bends and excessive tension on signal cables during packing and loading.  - Keeping sensitive electronics away from strong magnetic fields or heavy vibration in the vehicle.  - Ensuring that any equipment with backup batteries is transported in a way that avoids short circuits.  These can be short bullet points, but they will prevent a lot of hidden damage that only shows up later during installation.

I will update A4 to:  - Add an exception section for complex interference cases, with a clear stop point and escalation logging.  - Include a safety rule to stop work in unsafe environments, record the risk, and notify operations and the customer.  - Define mandatory logging of signal strength, signal-to-noise ratio where available, and all configuration changes.  With these changes, A4 should meet the requirements of T4 and give us the data we need for T9 and T10.  Unless there are objections, I plan to mark A4 as pilot-ready and record D5 once the updated version is shared.

For A6, I will incorporate:  - A clear rule that loads above manual limits require mechanical aids or extra staff, with the option to refuse unsafe moves.  - A step to coordinate with technicians to secure internal components or remove modules before transport when needed.  - A route assessment step for tight or risky paths, with guidance to stop and call operations if unsafe.  Combined with the telecom-specific points you both raised, this should make A6 robust enough for the pilot and aligned with T6.

Those updates sound good to me. With the added rules on heavy loads, route assessment, and coordination with technicians, I am comfortable using A6 in the pilot. It still looks practical enough for our current paper forms.

I agree with the changes you described for A4. The exception handling and safety rules are exactly what we need, and the mandatory readings list is clear. From my side, A4 is ready for pilot use. You can record D5 based on this.

Thanks both. I will now:  - Finalise A4 with the agreed exception and safety sections and mark it as pilot-ready under T4.  - Finalise A6 with the heavy load, route assessment, and telecom-specific handling points under T6.  I will record D5 and D6 as signed off for pilot use so we can include these procedures in the consolidated SOP later.

threads.thread_goal: Lock in scheduling rules and customer communication approach.

messages.text: With the diagnostic and SOP pieces in good shape, I have drafted proposals for Scheduling and Job Allocation Rules and the Customer Communication Playbook, stored as A5 and A7 under project_pack_ref: Field Service Workflow Standardisation for Repair Operations. These map to T5 and T7.  A5 covers: time slots, travel buffers, load limits for movers and technicians, and coordination rules between them. A7 covers: pre-visit notifications, on-site communication, delay handling, approvals, and post-visit follow-up.  We need to agree on: 1) The scheduling rules for the pilot routes (D7). 2) The communication approach for all pilot jobs (D8).  Please review A5 and A7 and comment on anything that looks unrealistic for day-to-day operations, especially around travel buffers and who owns which customer updates.

On A5, from the moving side:  - The proposed travel buffer of 30 minutes between jobs might be too generous on short city routes and too small on long rural ones. Maybe we can set a default buffer and allow operations to adjust by route type.  - Load limits per mover and per vehicle look reasonable, but we should make it clear that heavy or complex moves from A6 may require extra time slots.  - For coordination, I like the rule that movers should not wait more than a set time for technicians on-site before moving to the next job, as long as there is a clear way to record the missed handover.  On A7, it is important that when we are delayed, the person closest to the customer (often the technician) calls, but movers should still log delays that affect later jobs.

Looking at A5 from the appliance side:  - The time slots of 2 hours with a 20-minute buffer seem ok for most in-home jobs, but for complex appliances we might need a longer slot. Maybe we can tag some jobs as extended.  - The rule that we should not start a job if there is less than 45 minutes left in the slot is good, but we need a clear process in A7 for how we inform the customer and reschedule.  On A7:  - Pre-visit messages with a time window and basic prep instructions are helpful.  - For delays, I think technicians should call the customer directly, with a simple script, and customer service can follow up with a message if the delay is big.  - After the visit, a short summary of what was done and any next steps would help reduce repeat calls.

For workshop power tools, A5 mostly affects how movers bring tools in and how we plan bench time. A couple of thoughts:  - It would help if A5 required that tools for the same customer or site are grouped in the same run where possible, to reduce back-and-forth.  - For the pilot, maybe we can cap the number of new power tool jobs per day per technician, based on the time estimates we will capture in A3.  On A7, for approvals: I like the idea that technicians call the customer when extra damage is found, using a simple script, and then log the outcome. That should reduce confusion about costs and avoid rework.

From my side, the main thing is clarity. In A7, could we have very simple scripts or bullet points for the most common calls: confirming the visit, informing about a delay, and asking for approval for extra work? That would make it easier for me to handle calls without missing key information.  On A5, I do not have strong views, but I support grouping jobs and having clear limits on how many new jobs we take per day so we do not overbook.

For telecom and electronics visits, A5 and A7 look mostly fine, with a few tweaks:  - Time slots: 2-hour windows with a buffer work, but we should avoid stacking too many installs at the end of the day, since they often run long. Maybe A5 can limit late-day installs.  - Coordination with movers: when equipment is delivered separately, A5 should specify who confirms that everything has arrived before we start the job.  - In A7, for delays, I suggest we always send a quick message from customer service plus a call from the technician if the delay is more than 30 minutes. That combination tends to keep customers calmer.

Thanks for the detailed feedback. I will adjust A5 to:  - Define a default travel buffer, with guidance for operations to adjust by route type.  - Flag moves that follow A6 heavy or complex rules as requiring extended time slots.  - Set a standard maximum waiting time for movers at handover points, with a simple way to log missed handovers.  For A7, I will clarify that technicians own the direct customer call for delays, while movers and operations log delays that affect the rest of the route.

On the appliance side, I will update A5 and A7 to:  - Allow tagging some jobs as extended, with longer time slots.  - Add a rule that we do not start a job if there is less than 45 minutes left, and link that to a clear rescheduling and communication process in A7.  - In A7, include simple pre-visit messages, a short script for delay calls, and a brief post-visit summary template.  These changes should keep things realistic while still giving us structure for the pilot.

For power tools, I will:  - Add a rule in A5 to group tools from the same customer or site in the same run where possible.  - For the pilot, define a cap on new power tool jobs per technician per day, using the time estimates we will collect via A3.  In A7, I will include a simple script for calls about extra damage and cost approvals, with a field to log the outcome.  This should help us manage workload and reduce confusion about pricing.

For telecom and electronics, I will tweak A5 and A7 to:  - Limit late-day installs in the schedule.  - Clarify who confirms that all equipment has arrived before starting a job when movers are involved.  - In A7, define that for delays over 30 minutes, customer service sends a message and the technician calls.  I will also add simple scripts in A7 as requested, so everyone has clear wording for the most common situations.

With those adjustments, A5 looks workable from the moving side. The flexible buffer and clear waiting time rule will help us keep routes under control. I am ok with using these scheduling rules for the pilot routes.

I am comfortable with the updated approach in A5 and A7. The extended job tag and the clear rule about not starting late jobs, combined with the scripts for calls, should make it easier to explain things to customers. I support using these rules and templates in the pilot.

The grouping rule and job cap in A5 make sense to me. With the scripts in A7 for approvals, I feel more confident about calling customers about extra work. I agree with applying these scheduling and communication rules in the pilot.

From the telecom side, the updated A5 and A7 sound good. The limit on late-day installs and the combined message plus call for longer delays are practical. I am fine with locking these in for the pilot.

Thanks all. I will now:  - Finalise A5 with the agreed buffers, load limits, grouping rules, and coordination points, and mark it as the scheduling baseline for the pilot routes under T5.  - Finalise A7 with the scripts and ownership rules for pre-visit, delay, approval, and post-visit communication under T7.  I will record D7 and D8 as agreed so we can include these in the consolidated SOP and the pilot plan.

threads.thread_goal: Plan pilot, review results, and confirm adjustments before rollout.

messages.text: We have completed the pilot using the new SOP elements, checklists, and scheduling and communication rules. I have compiled the Pilot Results and Recommendations Report as A8 under project_pack_ref: Field Service Workflow Standardisation for Repair Operations, based on T9 and T10.  Highlights from A8:  - Rework rate dropped by about 18 percent across pilot jobs.  - Average time per job increased by around 7 percent, which is within our 10 percent limit.  - Missed or significantly delayed appointments decreased by roughly 20 percent on the pilot routes.  - Technician and customer feedback is mostly positive, with some suggestions to simplify parts of A2 and A3.  We now need to: 1) Reconfirm whether the top three problems we defined earlier have been addressed enough for this phase (D1). 2) Confirm the final version of the power tool checklist A3 for full rollout (D4), including any refinements from T11.  Please review A8, especially the sections relevant to your area, and share your view on what must change before full rollout and what can wait for a later iteration.

From the appliance side, A8 shows:  - Fewer repeat visits due to missed safety checks or incomplete diagnostics, which is good.  - Slightly longer average visit time, mainly because we are filling in A2 more carefully.  Feedback from my own jobs:  - The must-do safety checks in A2 are clear and easy to follow.  - The symptom-based diagnostic sections work, but for very simple issues, the checklist feels a bit long.  On the three main problems: 1) Diagnostics and logging are much better now. 2) Scheduling is improved, though there are still some tight days. 3) Customer communication is more consistent, especially around delays.  I think we have addressed them enough for this phase, with room to simplify A2 later.

Looking at A8 for power tools:  - Rework on pilot tools dropped noticeably, especially for cord damage and simple electrical faults.  - Job times increased a bit, but most of that is the extra time to fill in A3 and log readings.  From using A3 during the pilot and T11 refinements:  - The visual and electrical sections work well.  - The hints next to each mandatory test helped a lot, especially for colleagues less familiar with the instruments.  - The functional test under load is valuable, but for some tools it is hard to simulate a realistic load.  I propose we keep A3 mostly as is for rollout, with one change: allow a predefined list of reasons for skipping the load test, instead of free text, to speed up filling the form. With that, I am comfortable confirming A3 as final for D4.

From my experience in the pilot, A3 became easier to use after the hints were added. I still sometimes hesitate on which reason to write when skipping a load test, so having a predefined list as suggested would help me.  Overall, I feel more confident that I am not missing important steps. I support using the refined A3 for the full rollout, as long as the form stays clear and not too long.

On the telecom and electronics side, A8 shows:  - Better first-time fix rates, especially where we logged signal readings and configuration changes as per A4.  - Fewer escalations caused by missing data.  - Some extra time spent on logging, but still within acceptable limits.  Regarding the three main problems: 1) Standard diagnostics and logging are clearly improved. 2) Scheduling is more predictable, though we still had a few late-day installs running long. 3) Customer communication is more consistent, thanks to A7.  I would say we have addressed the three problems enough for this phase. The remaining issues are more about fine-tuning, not fundamental gaps.

From the moving side, A8 indicates:  - Fewer incidents with damage during transport, which I link to A6 being used more consistently.  - Better coordination with technicians on handovers, though there were still a few cases where we waited longer than planned.  On the three main problems: 1) Diagnostics and logging are better, which also helps us because intake information is clearer. 2) Scheduling and coordination improved, but we should keep refining buffers and route planning. 3) Customer communication is more structured, especially when delays affect multiple jobs.  I think we have made solid progress on all three, enough to move to rollout while continuing to adjust details.

Thanks for the appliance feedback.
